title: Failed-Part Bounty for Insurance Subrogation
one_liner: Pay plumbers a bounty to bag, photograph and chain-of-custody the pipe, supply line or fitting that failed, then sell the evidence and a brand-level failure database to insurers' subrogation units and manufacturers.
customer: Subrogation departments and subro vendors at regional and mutual homeowners insurers (the ones too small to send a forensic engineer to a $9k supply-line loss). Second buyers: plumbing manufacturers, distributors and private-label buyers who license the failure data.
problem: Water damage is among the top two homeowner claim categories. Product-defect subrogation (a supply line, PEX fitting, toilet connector, ice-maker line or water heater that failed early) only works if someone kept the failed part. The plumber is on scene 1 to 3 days before the adjuster, cuts the failed piece out, and tosses it in the truck-bed scrap bin. When the adjuster arrives the evidence is gone, the insurer eats the loss, and the manufacturer's lawyers cite spoliation. Insurers only hire the $2,000 forensic engineer on the big losses, so the routine $8-15k losses are never pursued. Meanwhile every plumber knows which brands are failing (certain plastic-nut braided lines, certain fill valves, certain fitting lots) but nobody aggregates it.
solution: A 90-second protocol and kit. Tamper-evident bag with a QR label, a phone flow (photo of the part in place, photo after removal, the manufacturer stamp or date code, homeowner e-signature by text, and the claim number if one exists). A weekly courier pickup from the shop and a climate-controlled evidence locker. Optional one-page factual cause-of-loss statement drawn from the same photos (sudden burst versus long-term seepage, which is exactly the 'gradual leak' exclusion that decides whether homeowners get paid). Every part is logged by brand, model, date code and failure mode, which builds a Backblaze-style public failure-rate report by product line. Insurers get the part plus a ready evidence package. The shop gets a bounty and a small line item on the invoice.
why_now: Water-loss severity has risen sharply and carriers are under pressure on homeowners loss ratios, so they are hunting for recovery dollars. Copper and steel tariffs plus the shift to PEX and imported fittings have flooded the market with cheaper components of unknown quality. Photo and OCR tooling now makes a cheap, standardized evidence workflow possible, and the subrogation trade press is openly saying evidence preservation is the make-or-break step.
revenue_model: Insurer or subro vendor pays $75-150 per part with a documented chain of custody, of which $40-60 goes to the shop and tech. Plus a 3-8% success share on any recovery that follows. Plus annual data licenses ($15-60k) to manufacturers, distributors and big-box private-label buyers, and per-report fees for expert-witness-ready packages.
non_obvious_insight: The evidence that decides tens of millions in recoveries is currently destroyed daily by the only people who touch it first, and the reason is not malice. Nobody pays a tech to spend 4 minutes and a bag on a piece of scrap. The plumber, not the adjuster, is the true first-notice-of-loss for the product itself. The bounty is a price signal, and the dataset that falls out is one nobody else can buy.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 shops through a local PHCC chapter and the owner Facebook and peer groups with a flat $50 per bag and a free kit. Design the label and the phone flow in a form tool. Collect the first 50 parts with photos. Take the first 20 case files to two regional mutual insurers and a subrogation vendor and ask them which they would have pursued. Sell a paid pilot for 100 parts on the strength of their answers.

judge_notes: operator: rank 7/25 - Sharp insight on destroyed evidence, but two-sided logistics and slow insurer buying delay first revenue.
contrarian: rank 3/25 - Plumber as true first notice of product failure is genuinely non-obvious; evidence bounty plus failure dataset is defensible.
vc: rank 1/24 - Truly non-obvious: plumber is first notice of loss for the part. Cheap to start, and the failure-data moat compounds.

competitors.name: Donan Engineering - Loss Logistics
competitors.what_they_do: Sells 'white-glove' evidence shipping, receiving, secure storage and single chain-of-custody with photo documentation at each stage, for insurers and forensic engineers. It sits inside a forensic engineering firm that also does water and flood investigations and component testing. It is engineer-assignment driven. There is no plumber-side capture, no per-part bounty, and no brand-level failure database on the pages I read.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established national forensic engineering firm. Funding and revenue not verified. No pricing published.

competitors.name: Envista Forensics and Rimkus (forensic engineering / property loss consulting)
competitors.what_they_do: Big forensic engineering and claims consulting firms that would be the default answer for a large product-failure loss. Their sites list failure analysis, equipment consulting and property loss consulting. Neither site mentions evidence storage, chain-of-custody kits or any low-cost program for routine $8-15k water losses. That gap is the wedge the idea targets. They are also the incumbents who could copy a lightweight protocol.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Large established firms. Sizes and funding not verified. Rimkus URL: https://www.rimkus.com

competitors.name: LeakBot
competitors.what_they_do: Insurer-funded leak detection with free repairs by employee plumbers, offered as a no-cost policyholder benefit. Named insurer partners on the page are Nationwide, PURE, Selective and Admiral. It shows insurers already pay for plumber-delivered services, and it holds a plumber network with claim context at dispatch. The page never mentions subrogation, failed parts or evidence capture. It could add this as a feature.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Multiple named US and UK insurer partners. Funding not verified.

competitors.name: ServiceTitan and CompanyCam (plumber field software)
competitors.what_they_do: These are the tools plumbers already use for forms, photos and equipment history. ServiceTitan has Forms, Equipment Management and 'Field Findings'. CompanyCam is a photo documentation app. Neither page I read shows a failed-part or chain-of-custody workflow. They are the likeliest incumbents to add a checkbox feature. CompanyCam: https://companycam.com
competitors.scale_or_funding: ServiceTitan is a public company with a very large plumbing customer base. CompanyCam is a large venture-backed SMB contractor app. Figures not verified.

competitors.name: CPSC SaferProducts.gov
competitors.what_they_do: A free public database of consumer product incident reports that anyone can submit to. Manufacturers are notified and may post comments. It is unstructured and self-reported, with no physical evidence, no date-code discipline and no plumbing-specific failure rates. It is a free substitute for the public 'which brand fails' data, but a weak one.

competition.white_space:
Caveat: the session's WebSearch budget ran out (200 of 200) before any search ran. This verdict rests on direct page fetches of about a dozen vendor, industry and government sites, plus two empty GitHub searches. I did not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or trade press, so I could not rule out a small funded startup doing exactly this. Run 4-6 searches before committing money. Suggested queries: 'subrogation evidence preservation plumber', 'failed part bounty', 'water loss evidence kit', and the same on Crunchbase.

What I found is a real gap in what I could reach. Evidence logistics and forensic engineering exist for engineer-assigned losses (Donan, Envista, Rimkus). Insurer-funded plumber networks exist (LeakBot). Plumber field software exists (ServiceTitan, CompanyCam). No page I read describes any of these paying or equipping the plumber to retain the failed part on routine sub-$15k water losses. The public failure data I found is weak (SaferProducts.gov). Nothing I found is a date-code and brand-level failure-rate dataset.

Unserved specifically: (1) plumber-side capture at the moment of removal, including a per-part payment. (2) A neutral custodian and evidence package for the $8-15k tier, which is below the point where a $2k engineer is dispatched. (3) A structured brand, model and date-code failure dataset from real removed parts.

The main risks are structural, not competitive. (a) The plumber often arrives before a claim exists, so the claim number and the bounty payer are unknown at bagging. (b) Mitigation contractors and insurer-dispatched vendors may reach the site first on many losses. (c) The recovery economics of small product-defect claims are unproven, so insurers may not pay $75-150 for parts they would not pursue anyway. (d) A public brand-level failure report invites manufacturer legal pushback. (e) A 'cause-of-loss statement' from a tech risks unlicensed-engineering objections. (f) I could not fetch HomeServe (403), so I cannot say whether that plumber-network incumbent already does something like this.
competition.evidence_of_demand:
Verified, problem size only: the Insurance Information Institute reports water damage and freezing claims at 22.6% of homeowners claims in 2023, at about 1.50 claims per 100 house-years, with average severity of about $15,400 (https://www.iii.org/fact-statistic/facts-statistics-homeowners-and-renters-insurance). That matches the idea's $8-15k loss tier.

Verified, spend on adjacent services: (1) Donan sells evidence shipping, storage and chain-of-custody as a dedicated paid service (http://donan.com/product-intelligence-liability/loss-logistics), so insurers pay for evidence custody on larger losses. (2) LeakBot's insurer partners (Nationwide, PURE, Selective, Admiral) pay for plumber-delivered services and claims-mitigation reports (https://www.leakbot.io), so insurers will fund plumber networks.

Not verified this session: trade press saying evidence preservation is make-or-break, forum complaints from adjusters or plumbers, RFPs, and any insurer already paying per part. I found no direct evidence that anyone pays per failed part or buys a plumber-sourced brand failure dataset. The first-30-days plan (ask two mutual insurers which of the 20 case files they would have pursued) is the right way to test this.
competition.sharper_angle:
Do not build a marketplace that buys parts from every plumber. Build a neutral evidence custodian embedded in channels where the claim number and the payer are already known at dispatch.

1. Start with insurer-dispatched and insurer-funded plumber programs (emergency plumbing and leak-response networks, preferred-vendor programs, home-warranty and service-plan networks). The insurer controls the vendor, so the bounty and bag become a contracted line item in the dispatch workflow. There is no cold-start recruiting of independent shops and no orphaned parts with no claim.
2. Limit the wedge to 4-5 part types where product-defect subrogation is strongest and the part is small and cheap to ship: braided supply lines, ice-maker lines, toilet connectors, PEX fittings, water heater components.
3. Position as a neutral, joint-exam-ready custodian (documented protocol, notice to all interested parties, photo and QR chain of custody, homeowner e-sign). Insurers get admissible evidence, and manufacturers cannot easily cite spoliation. Do not sell a cause-of-loss opinion. Provide factual photo records and route to licensed engineers, or partner with one such as Donan-type firms as the escalation path.
4. Sell first to subrogation vendors and recovery law firms that work on contingency and need the part before they take a $10k file. Their willingness to advance $75-150 per part is the fastest demand test.
5. Keep the failure dataset private and consortium-style for participating insurers, with anonymized aggregate reporting by product line and date code. Skip a public Backblaze-style brand naming until there is enough volume and legal review. License to manufacturers only after that.
6. Before building, run the cheap kill test: hand-collect 50 parts, take 20 case files to two mutual insurers and one subrogation vendor, and get a written 'we would have pursued these' count and a per-part price. Also finish the missing searches (Crunchbase, YC, trade press) that this run could not do.
